teaser: iason's comparison of four AI risk frameworks, mapped to the behaviour policy, the footprint and the graphs that run here, with the status of each row.
core_idea: The OECD classification, the NIST AI RMF, Japan's guidelines and the EU AI Act converge on five principles, as iason's paper says, but their unit is an AI system classified before deployment; for an agent the unit is one agent in one deployment, described by a written behaviour policy, measured by its footprint and blast radius, and each framework's question has a mechanism here that runs, is designed or is argued, which the mapping file published with the article records row by row.

nodes.label: iason's four-framework paper
nodes.summary: AI Risk Management Frameworks, November 2025: the OECD classification, the NIST AI RMF, Japan's guidelines and the EU AI Act, converging on five principles.

nodes.label: The unit is one agent in one deployment
nodes.summary: The frameworks classify an AI system before deployment; an agent's risk is its reach in a given setup, not a property of the model.

nodes.label: The behaviour policy
nodes.summary: Reach measured, mandate written, the gap typed by what stands in the way, written before the agent runs and restored after every summary.

nodes.label: Footprint and blast radius
nodes.summary: What the agent did, read afterwards from logs, and what each row would cost if used in full today.

nodes.label: OECD: five dimensions
nodes.summary: People and Planet, Economic Context, Data and Input, AI Model, Task and Output; the last two matter most for an agent.

nodes.label: NIST: govern, map, measure, manage
nodes.summary: Fifteen numbered outcomes, each with a mechanism here and the article where it runs.

nodes.label: Japan: three roles
nodes.summary: Developer, provider and business user: the model vendor, the platform and the deployer of an agent.

nodes.label: The EU AI Act: tier, word, dates
nodes.summary: Obligations by tier; residual risk 'judged to be acceptable' undefined; application dates moved after the paper.

nodes.label: Oversight by reversibility
nodes.summary: A person where an output cannot be undone, controls that do not get tired elsewhere, one position per output rather than per system.

nodes.label: Accepted is not acceptable
nodes.summary: A risk has a holder, an interval and the facts that would end it; three doors and no deny button.

nodes.label: A policy beside the prompt
nodes.summary: The contract between vendor, platform and deployer: published, accepted, enforced where it can be, breaches reported.

nodes.label: The paper needs a status since
nodes.summary: Written before Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 moved the Act's dates and before software became a product under EU liability rules.

nodes.label: Three graphs already hold two of the four
nodes.summary: The Act parsed into a vault; a control framework joined to the Act's text; a ten-layer stack with 119 edges from provisions.

nodes.label: The mapping file
nodes.summary: Thirty-two rows, each framework element against what answers it here, where to check, and whether it runs, is designed or is argued.

nodes.label: The mandate is the hard part
nodes.summary: Observation tells you what an agent did; only a written mandate tells you whether it was allowed.

quotes.text: Observation tells you what an agent did. Only a written mandate tells you whether it was allowed, and without one every finding in the footprint is a judgement call and every deflection in the liability line is available.
quotes.why: The answer to which part of governance is hardest, from this record.

quotes.text: The same model that drafts an email with no way to send it, and the same model with a send button and a customer database, are not the same system, and no tier assigned to the model tells you which one you have.
quotes.why: Why the unit has to be one agent in one deployment.

figures.caption: Four frameworks, as iason's paper reads them, against what runs here. For each: the question it asks of a system, how the paper summarises it, what answers it on this site and at RiskMandate, the article or vault where that can be checked, and whether it runs, is designed or is only argued. Green runs; amber is a design; grey is an argument.

Two units. On the left, the frameworks' unit: an AI system, described by its characteristics, context and impact, given a tier, and assigned obligations, before it is deployed. On the right, the unit here: one agent in one deployment, with its reach measured, its mandate written, the gap between them typed by what stands in the way, its footprint read afterwards, and a blast radius for every row. The arrows show where each of the four frameworks attaches.

A status since, for the paper. Above the line, the dates as the paper gives them, as of November 2025: prohibitions in force from February 2025, and the rules applying in full by August 2026. Below the line, what this site's own articles recorded afterwards: the amending regulation in force from 27 July 2026, Annex III obligations from 2 December 2027, Annex I from 2 August 2028, and software a product under the EU's new liability rules from 9 December 2026. Neither row is wrong on its day.

The paper's five shared principles, each against what answers it here, the evidence, and how far it goes: runs, in green; a published design with a demo behind it, in amber. Four of the five run, on one newsroom and one agent team; risk acceptance as a record is the design.
